entries.title: Javier Assad wraps first half as one of Cubs’ pitching lifesavers, but team’s quest for health far from over
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI – The Reds knocked back-to-back jacks off <b>Javier Assad</b> on Saturday night.</p><p>But by then, the righty’s work in helping keep the Cubs’ injury-ravaged pitching staff afloat had already made him one of this team’s first-half lifesavers.</p><p>“It’s been a time of need for us in the rotation. When you have injuries and you bring guys up to add to your rotation, he has more than delivered from that role,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said before the game. “That’s been a really positive development in the midst of a lot of injuries.</p><p>“He has taken advantage of an opportunity and given us strong innings. Whether it’s been starting or the bullpen, he’s given us very strong innings.”</p><p>Assad’s performance has indeed been big as the Cubs have tried to navigate an injury avalanche that at one point saw an entire rotation and late-inning relief mix on the shelf simultaneously.</p><p>Sent to the minors in mid May with an ERA near 6.00, the Cubs called on him when righty <b>Jameson Taillon</b> went down in the middle of a start. Assad delivered what Counsell called a “heroic” 6 1/3 innings in relief, allowing only one hit.</p><p>Plugged into the rotation, Assad has a 2.39 ERA in five starts since – including the two runs on two solo homers he allowed in five innings Saturday – and also logged another multi-inning relief outing.</p><p>The innings Assad has provided would have been valuable enough, given the need. The performance has made him part of the reason those injuries haven’t buried the team.</p><p>Of course, the All-Star break is not a finish line, and the Cubs are far from out of the woods when it comes to getting healthy.</p><p>“We’re not going to come back from the break and be finished with the injuries,” Counsell said Friday. “We’ve still got injury issues. … Every team has some injuries, but to get back to medium strength, we’re still at a pretty big deficit after the break.”</p><p>Taillon is due back soon after he threw 4 2/3 scoreless innings in a rehab start Saturday. But the Cubs will still be waiting on recoveries from starter <b>Edward Cabrera</b>, closer <b>Daniel Palencia</b> and multiple relievers, including lefty <b>Hoby Milner</b>. Lefty <b>Justin Steele</b> and righty <b>Ben Brown</b> are also sidelined, perhaps not expected to return in time to make starts before season’s end.</p><p>It’s what has made Assad – and others who weren’t supposed to shoulder starring roles – such a valuable contributor. The depth he’s provided could serve the Cubs well as they eye a deep postseason run.</p><p><b>Big night for bullpen</b></p><p>The Cubs got four innings of one-run ball from their relievers in Saturday’s 5-3 win over the Reds, with righty <b>Trent Thornton</b>’s fist pump after getting the final out an exclamation point.</p><p>“I’m a pretty emotional pitcher more times than not,” Thornton said.</p><p>Thornton has had plenty to celebrate, picking up three saves as one of several surprise success stories in a bullpen hit hard by injuries.</p><p>Saturday, he was called on to get the final out, preserving a two-run lead with a game-ending grounder with two runners in scoring position.</p><p>“He’s just got guts,” Counsell said.</p><p>Thornton’s three saves this season are three times as many as he had in his career coming into the season.</p><p>“I’m not going to complain at all,” he said. “As long as we’re getting the job done and winning games, that’s all that matters at the end of the day. It doesn’t matter whose hand it’s coming out of.</p><p>“There’s a lot of guys in this bullpen with saves this year. It’s pretty cool.”</p><p><b>Maton returns</b></p><p>The Cubs are happy to have righty reliever <b>Phil Maton</b> back from the IL, hoping the knee tendinitis that has perhaps contributed to his poor performance – he woke up Saturday with an ERA north of 6.00 – is behind him.</p><p>“The knee has affected him, there’s no question about it,” Counsell said. “He would tell you it hasn’t always prevented him from pitching, but it’s just there.</p><p>“We’ve taken two tries now to try to get it behind him a little bit and put it in the background. It’s going to be there a little bit as we move forward, but hopefully, we can kind of keep it in the background.”</p>

entries.title: Rev. Michael Pfleger removed from St. Sabina Church amid investigation into decades-old sex abuse claim
entries.summary: <p>The Rev. Michael Pfleger has been removed from his ministry at St. Sabina Church as the Archdiocese of Chicago investigates a claim of child sexual abuse from more than 30 years ago.</p><p>It’s the fifth decades-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/15/23406159/father-pfleger-sex-abuse-allegations-misconduct-second-archdiocese-chicago-sabina" target="_blank" >accusation</a> against the South Side priest in four years. Pfleger was cleared of the other accusations.</p><p>In a letter to parishioners Saturday, Cardinal Blase Cupich said the alleged abuse happened at St. Sabina Church more than 30 years ago. He said Pfleger “strongly denied” the accusation.</p><p>In a written statement, Pfleger called the allegation, "an absolute lie." </p><p>Pfleger said he was informed of the accusation Thursday by the vicar of priests and told the accuser is a woman who went to school at St. Sabina and that she said she was sexually abused by Pfleger sometime between 1993 and 1995, when she was a minor. </p><p>Pfleger said the accusation is "another attack by those who have sought to destroy me for years and another attempt by someone to get money from the archdiocese and to silence me.</p><p>"Let me be clear, sexual abuse is wrong, and I realize that the Catholic church has a long history of not dealing with accusations and has spent a number of years putting strong policies in place, but I have said countless times I believe the current policy is wrong and unfair to the accused priest," Pfleger said. </p><p>While delivering the "difficult news" to parishioners, Cupich wrote, “I want to stress that the welfare of the children entrusted to our care is our paramount concern.</p><p>“The Archdiocese of Chicago takes all allegations of sexual misconduct seriously. We appreciate the courage it takes to step forward and encourage anyone who believes they have experienced abuse or inappropriate behavior by a member of the clergy, religious or lay employee of the archdiocese to report it to the Office for the Protection of Children and Youth.”</p><p>The Archdiocese of Chicago’s Independent Review Board is investigating and will make a recommendation to Cupich.</p><p>The Rev. Thulani Magwaza will continue to serve as pastor of St. Sabina Parish, Cupich said.</p><p>Pfleger was first removed from St. Sabina in January 2021 after being accused of sexually abusing a minor more than 40 years earlier. Later that month, the brother of Pfleger’s first accuser came forward with his own accusations.</p><p>After a five-month investigation into the claims involving the brothers, an archdiocese review board found “insufficient reason to suspect Father Pfleger is guilty of these allegations.” Pfleger returned to Sunday service in June 2021.</p><p>Then, in March 2022, a 59-year-old man came forward to bolster the brothers’ claims, saying Pfleger molested him at St. Sabina when the man was 18.</p><p>In October 2022, a man in his late 40s said Pfleger sexually abused him twice in the late 1980s.</p><p>Pfleger, 77, has been the pastor at St. Sabina Church since 1981 and has become a leading voice against violence.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/4/21/22396614/cardinal-blase-cupich-st-sabina-michael-pfleger-abuse-church-sex" >Cupich accuses St. Sabina of ‘inappropriate and intimidating tactics’ toward Pfleger abuse investigators</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2022/5/20/23125545/michael-sneed-father-pfleger-st-sabina-juneteenth-march-anti-gun-violence-trump" >Pfleger still at forefront of anti-gun fight as he plans June march</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/4/22/22398276/after-warning-from-cardinal-st-sabina-pastor-says-hes-encouraging-respectful-support-for-pfleger" >After warning from cardinal, St. Sabina pastor says he’s encouraging ‘respectful’ support for Pfleger</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: What do Chicago teens need to feel welcome Downtown? Four shared their ideas
entries.summary: <p>In Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://www.formyblock.org/downtownday" target="_blank" >Downtown Day</a> allows teens to feel welcome, safe and seen in the city, but many say they wish that was the case year-round.</p><p>They expressed that opinion on Saturday at the annual event, which brings more than 1,000 young people from the South and West Sides into the city for workshops, tours and activities. </p><p>The initiative is hosted by youth empowerment nonprofit My Block, My Hood, My City, which partners with more than 30 businesses and organizations, including the Art Institute of Chicago, Navy Pier, Shedd Aquarium and Water Tower Place, to offer the experiences. (This year, WBEZ was also listed among the participants.) Each teen receives a $50 prepaid debit card to use at destinations of their choice.</p><p>The event happened amid growing concerns about so-called “teen takeovers,” or large gatherings of young people that are coordinated on social media. Some have turned violent, due in part to easy access to guns, while others have occurred without incident. </p><p>The events have commanded the attention of Chicago's City Council, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/24/teen-takeovers-chicago-city-council-hearing-youth-testimony" >hosted a hearing</a> on the topic in June. Last summer, the governing body responded by passing a stricter curfew ordinance, but it was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/07/16/snap-curfew-veto-upheld-mayor-johnson-city-council-vote" >ultimately vetoed </a>by Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>“A lot of the communities that teens are from are disinvested, and we're pushing them out of spaces,” said Briana Mathews, manager of youth development at My Block, My Hood My City.</p><p>But Downtown Day provides a model for them to feel welcome and give them agency to curate their own entertainment, she said.</p><p>“Once we start treating them like they are partners and collaborators, then we can see them thrive,” she explained.</p><p>With that in mind, we asked several teens to share their favorite activities, concerns and ideas for new opportunities. entries.summary: <p>While FBI Director Kash Patel reportedly canceled his flight to Chicago after a last-minute White House summons, his girlfriend, country music singer Alexis Wilkins, sprinkled in a few patriotic moments during her performance Saturday at Windy City Smokeout.</p><p>An American flag hung from the drummer’s set, with red, white and blue lighting often illuminating the stage under the sunny, afternoon sky outside the United Center.</p><p>At one point, Wilkins told the crowd this was her first time in Chicago, adding, “I love this city.”</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Why Blackhawks GM Kyle Davidson will defy analytics to bet on a hunch
entries.summary: <p>Bowen Byram, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*6w99bc*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTgxMzg5NTU2My4xNzgzNjMxNDg1*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODM2MzE0ODQkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODM2MzE1MDUkajM5JGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' new No. 1 defenseman, and Mason West, one of their many forward prospects, are not remotely similar players — neither in age, caliber nor position.</p><p>But for Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson, Byram and West are two data points that form the start of a pattern.</p><p>Davidson's impassioned <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/06/24/blackhawks-bowen-byram-elite-defenseman-chicago-trade-kyle-davidson?_gl=1*1qf0enw*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTgxMzg5NTU2My4xNzgzNjMxNDg1*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODM2MzE0ODQkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODM2MzE0OTckajQ3JGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >explanations</a> and justifications of his trade for Byram — which represented something of a break in character for a man who likes to set expectations low and isn't usually brash with words — are actually reminiscent of his justification for trading up to pick West in the 2025 draft.</p><p>It was the end of a long, eventful, tiring June night when Davidson met with reporters after the first round of that 2025 draft, and it's common for NHL GMs to be most honest and unfiltered in situations like that (when their brains are fried).</p><p>Davidson certainly was when discussing his decision to give the Hurricanes two extra picks — second- and fifth-rounders — just to move up from 34th to 29th to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/07/20/blackhawks-mason-west-nhl-prospects-hockey-football-edina-fargo-michigan-state" target="_blank" >select West</a>. The resulting quotes were some of the most memorable of his GM tenure.</p><p>"I don't know what you call it, the stats or the analytics of it, [but] the trade we made to get back in the first round was not that," Davidson said then. "I gave up probably a lot more to get back in to take Mason than the charts would suggest. And that's OK. Sometimes we're willing to do that and I'm willing to stick my neck out and really jump at a guy.</p><p>"I just really wanted to get back into the first round and take what I thought was a grand-slam hack. I was swinging for the fences and figured, 'Why not? Let's go for a big one here.'"</p><p>Davidson's more recent decision to give the Sabres the fourth overall pick, plus beloved defenseman Louis Crevier and a second-round pick, for Byram (and salary-dump forward Jordan Greenway) fell in a similar bucket.</p><p>No analytics model considered it close to equal value — not the public models, and likely not the Hawks' internal model, either.</p><p>Fourth overall for Byram, a former fourth overall pick himself, might've been close to equal, but the other involved pieces tipped the scales. The huge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/01/blackhawks-bowen-byram-contract-nhl-defensemen-free-agency?_gl=1*z3v5hx*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTgxMzg5NTU2My4xNzgzNjMxNDg1*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODM2MzE0ODQkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODM2MzE0ODQkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >contract extension</a> the Hawks then gave Byram — carrying a $12.5 million salary-cap hit — was also considered a heavy overpay by analytics models.</p><p>The Hawks have invested a lot in analytics — their nine-person department, filled with data scientists and engineers, is one of the league's largest — and some critics questioned the purpose of that investment if the Hawks are going to make moves like this anyway.</p><p>But the Byram gamble largely came down to Davidson deciding, on another one-time basis, to ignore analytics and logic and take a grand-slam swing. His willingness to occasionally do that is becoming one of his signature quirks, distinguishing him from his GM peers.</p><p>It will take time to determine whether that quirk will prove fruitful for Davidson or instead undo the careful asset collection he spends the other 364 days of every year on.</p><p>When asked about the emerging pattern, though, he didn't shy away from admitting to it. The fact the question came at the end of another long, eventful, tiring day — this time July 1, the start of free agency — might have again contributed to his response's candor.</p><p>"I don’t believe that that’s something that you want to do consistently," Davidson said. "But when appropriate, and when you’ve got someone there who you truly do believe in and you want to be aggressive toward, then I believe there is a lot of value just getting your guy and bringing them into your group.</p><p>"If you do that in every move, you’re going to lose out on that equation over the long haul. You don’t want to make a habit of it. </p><p>"But...there’s not many opportunities to get certain players that you really believe in, because they just don’t become available that often — whether in the draft or trade or whatever. Good players are very hard to come by. When you do believe and you do have an open lane to try to do something, I believe it's incumbent on you to act and make it happen."</p><p>He continued on for a while longer, adding that the strategy "may be not for everyone, but it’s my inclination to get it done."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Getty Images/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A talking point around the league this summer has regarded how it's more difficult to build a team up than tear it down. It's especially harder in this current environment, since there are currently so few tearing-it-down teams to partner with on would-be mutually beneficial trades.</p><p>Davidson has now entered that harder stage, and he's hearing criticism for his approach so far — not only for the Byram trade in a vacuum, but also for doing that instead of finding an established top-six forward to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/02/blackhawks-first-line-hole-connor-bedard-kyle-davidson-nhl-trades?_gl=1*1d86ci5*_up*MQ..*_ga*MjY4NDYyMTYuMTc4MzYzMzQ0MA..*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODM2MzM0NDAkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODM2MzM0ODMkajE3JGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >help</a> Connor Bedard.</p><p>Now that Bedard is slated to miss the first month or two of the regular season recovering from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/08/blackhawks-connor-bedard-shoulder-surgery-injury-timeline?_gl=1*12lik2k*_up*MQ..*_ga*MjY4NDYyMTYuMTc4MzYzMzQ0MA..*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODM2MzM0NDAkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODM2MzM0NDAkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >shoulder surgery</a>, it will be interesting to see if Davidson pivots to adding another forward or if he patiently waits for Bedard's return. A reunion with Patrick Kane, who's currently a free agent, does seem possible.</p><p>Sharks GM Mike Grier, formerly a darling of the analytics community (to an almost absurd degree), has also taken heat lately for acquiring and overpaying Keifer Sherwood, for overpaying Jacob Trouba and for acquiring overpaid Darnell Nurse.</p><p>It's no coincidence this heat coincides with Grier entering his own build-up era. It's also worth noting Grier's strong interest in Byram reportedly forced the Hawks to improve their offer to get him — they might've been able to keep, say, Crevier otherwise.</p><p>Over the next few years, it might prove to be that no GM can look good during an early build-up era within this extreme sellers' market. Perhaps nobody can win these kinds of trades in the court of public opinion.</p><p>Perhaps the teams that emerge successfully from rebuilds in the 2020s — as the Canadiens are doing now — are going to be the teams whose big risks paid off, not the teams who avoided big risks.</p><p>That would still leave the Hawks dependent on Davidson's hunches proving correct. But at least Davidson, for one, believes wholeheartedly, fervently and unconditionally in those hunches.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Struggling daughter seems uninterested in helping herself
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am the single mom of a 19-year-old daughter who copes with bipolar 2, ADHD, anxiety and depression. She has a mental age that's younger than her adult self. Over the years, she has gone through therapy and changes in medication.</p><p>It has been recommended that my daughter attend a residential therapy program, but she refuses. Since finishing high school, she has refused everything: college classes, job applications, exploring other therapies or taking any small steps toward independence in the future.</p><p>Her goals now center around socializing and smoking marijuana with a few friends. She rarely leaves her room except when they call. There are days I doubt she's med compliant or wants the help others try to give.</p><p>It's heartbreaking watching her being "stuck," but I am also tired of being held hostage to her behavior and actions. Many days I want to pack up her stuff and tell myself she'll figure things out. (I would continue to be here when she needs me.) Is this fair given her mental health challenges? Because she is at risk, I feel like anything I do is wrong. — <i>BURNED-OUT MOM IN COLORADO</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOM:</b> I know of few people who, if given the choice, wouldn't like life to be a constant party. You may need the services of a licensed psychotherapist to decide what to do to help your daughter. It's apparent to me that unless there are consequences for her unwillingness to help herself, nothing will change and she will continue floating on a cloud of cannabis in perpetuity.</p><p>I suggest you make her continuing to live with you contingent upon her participation in the program that will help her gain some independence. If you need more guidance about this, contact NAMI — the National Alliance on Mental Illness. It's the nation's largest mental health organization, dedicated to building better lives for the millions of Americans affected by mental illness. You will find more information about it at nami.org.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mother died five years ago, and my stepfather passed away a month ago. Both were cremated with no service, no obituary and no celebration of life. My parents' wish was to be placed together at their home.</p><p>I asked my brother, stepsister and stepbrother if I could have a small amount of their ashes to place in a small urn or a piece of memorial jewelry. My stepbrother is fine with my request; the other two are appalled.</p><p>I am the oldest, but my stepfather gave my brother power of attorney. I think this authority has gone to his head, as he tells us he is the boss. Was it wrong to request some of my parents' ashes? — <i>GRIEVING DAUGHTER</i></p><p><b>DEAR GRIEVING DAUGHTER:</b> Please accept my condolences for the loss of your parents. Of course your request was not wrong or even unusual. Families often divide a loved one's ashes just as you described. If your brother continues to ignore your appeals as a grieving sibling, you must decide whether this is important enough to bring a lawyer into the discussion.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O.
